stem: A client arrives in the PACU after general anesthesia. The client is markedly drowsy, is breathing spontaneously, is not clearing pooled oral secretions, and reports incisional pain. Which nursing action is the priority?

options.A: Inspect the surgical dressing and drain output before reassessing the client's respiratory status.
options.B: Assess airway patency and suction the pooled oral secretions as indicated while monitoring respiration.
options.C: Administer the prescribed analgesic and reassess respiratory status after the pain improves.
options.D: Begin coached coughing and deep-breathing exercises before addressing the pooled oral secretions.

rationale: During Phase I postanesthesia recovery, airway monitoring takes precedence as the client emerges from anesthesia. A markedly drowsy client who is not clearing pooled oral secretions requires assessment of airway patency and suctioning of the secretions as indicated while respiratory status is monitored. Dressing and drain assessment, pain treatment, and pulmonary-hygiene exercises are important postoperative interventions, but none should delay management of an immediate airway-clearance concern.
educational_objective: In early PACU recovery, prioritize airway assessment and secretion clearance over other important postoperative interventions when a drowsy client cannot clear oral secretions.
source_organization: Open Resources for Nursing (Open RN) / Chippewa Valley Technical College; hosted by NCBI Bookshelf
source_locator: Section 2.5 Postoperative Nursing Care > Care in the Post-Anesthesia Care Unit or Intensive Care Unit: Phase I close monitoring of the airway, vital signs, and recovery indicators takes precedence as clients emerge from anesthesia; Table 2.5c, respiratory interventions: perform suctioning as indicated to clear airways of secretions.
source_claim_supported: In Phase I PACU recovery, airway monitoring takes precedence, and postoperative suctioning is used as indicated to clear airway secretions.

supporting_sources.organization: Open Resources for Nursing (Open RN) / Chippewa Valley Technical College; hosted by NCBI Bookshelf
supporting_sources.document_title: Nursing Skills [Internet], 2nd edition, Chapter 22: Tracheostomy Care & Suctioning
supporting_sources.locator: Sections 22.1-22.4: oral suction removes oral secretions; maintaining a patent airway is a top priority; suctioning is used in postoperative care and is indicated when a patient cannot clear secretions or has visible secretions that persist.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Oral/oropharyngeal suctioning is appropriate when a client cannot clear accumulated oral secretions, with respiratory assessment and monitoring around suctioning.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Appendix A, Physiological Adaptation, p. 46: Provide postoperative care; Perform suctioning; Provide pulmonary hygiene; Manage the care of a client with impaired ventilation/oxygenation.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — postoperative airway assessment and secretion clearance
correction_summary: Rebuilt the item to remove the uniquely-long correct-answer cue, absolute/implausible distractors, and unsupported universal positioning language. The corrected item tests a single PACU airway-priority decision with source-supported secretion clearance and balanced, clinically relevant distractors.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Postanesthesia airway protection and secretion clearance
audit_findings.stem: PASS — realistic PACU context, explicit inability to clear pooled secretions, no hidden positioning assumption.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — dressing/drain assessment is relevant postoperative care but is lower priority than an active airway-clearance concern.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS — directly addresses airway patency and the client's inability to clear pooled oral secretions; source-supported and uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — analgesia is relevant postoperative care but does not precede management of the airway-clearance concern.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — pulmonary hygiene is relevant postoperative care but does not replace immediate clearance of pooled secretions the drowsy client is not clearing.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — no defensible second best answer after correction.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A, C, and D are legitimate postoperative interventions but are incorrect in the stated priority sequence.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — option lengths are comparable; no absolute-word or uniquely-long-correct-answer pattern remains.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation explicitly includes postoperative care, suctioning, pulmonary hygiene, and impaired ventilation/oxygenation management.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged suction versus pulmonary hygiene, pain treatment, and routine postoperative assessment; the explicit failure to clear pooled oral secretions preserves one source-supported priority answer without unsupported precision.
